bodyHtml:
Maltese is a Semitic language and is the national language of Malta, where it is spoken by about 560,000 people. Along with English it is an official language in Malta, and is also one of the European Union's official languages. Here are some nouns in Maltese given along with their definite articles ("the").

il lanġas
(the pear)
li mħadda
(the pillow)
is sħana
(the heat)
il mara
(the woman)
iċ ċpar
(the mist)
il ġobon
(the cheese)
li ksieħ
(the cold)
l għonq
(the neck)
il bar
(the bar)
l art
(the earth)
li ħmar
(the donkey)
id dar
(the house)
li bdiewa
(the peasants)
l uffiċċju
(the office)
iż żir
(the jug)
il lvant
(the east)
ir raġel
(the man)
il ktieb
(the book)
l jum
(the day)
il vjola
(the violet)
is silġ
(the snow)
il qassis
(the priest)

As you can see, Maltese has some consonants that are different from those of English. To help you understand how these consonants are pronounced, here is some information on their location in the mouth and manner of articulation.

LabialAlveolarPalatalVelarPharyngealGlottal
Nasalmn
Stopp, bt, dk, gq
Affricateċ, ġ, z
Fricativef, vs, ż, xħ
Semivowelj
Trill/Lateralr, l

Notes:

  • labial = with the lips, alveolar = with the tip of the tongue, palatal = with the hard palate of the mouth, velar = with the soft palate of the mouth, pharyngeal = with the pharynx of the throat, glottal = with the glottis
  • nasal = through the nose, stop = with stopped airflow, fricative = with friction, affricate = stop followed by fricative, semivowel = like a shorter vowel, trill = with the tongue vibrating, lateral = with air though the sides of the mouth
  • Also, the letter h and combination għ are silent (not pronounced)

A1. Two of the words above don't follow the normal rules of Maltese. What are these two words? Mark them down on the answer sheets.

A2. Give the appropriate form of the definite article for the following nouns on the answer sheets. All of these nouns follow the normal rules of Maltese.

xkora(sack)
ġebla(stone)
mniħer(nose)
xemx(sun)
kafè(coffee)
hena(happiness)
għajn(eye)
tama(hope)
ors(bear)
missier(father)
lura(back)
ilma(water)
beraq(lightning)
nar(fire)
nifs(breath)
dlam(darkness)

questions.partPrompt: Two of the words above don't follow the normal rules of Maltese. What are these two words?
Give the appropriate form of the definite article for the following nouns. All of these nouns follow the normal rules of Maltese.

hints.text: The article never depends on the meaning of the noun. Sort the 22 given examples by which article they take, then look only at how each noun begins - and check that first letter against the consonant chart.

There are four cases, and they have to be tried in order. Ask first: does the noun start with a consonant from the alveolar column of the chart? If so the article's consonant is replaced by a copy of that consonant. If not, ask whether the noun starts with a vowel or with a silent letter (remember h and għ are silent, and j behaves like a vowel here) - those get the shortest article. If not, ask whether the noun starts with two consonants in a row. Anything left over gets the default form.

Try the rule out on data you are not being graded on. In is sħana (the heat) the noun starts with s, which sits in the alveolar column, so the article's consonant becomes a copy of s; iż żir (the jug) works the same way with ż. Compare iċ ċpar (the mist): ċ is an affricate, but it is still in the alveolar column, so it copies too. Now notice that ir raġel and li ħmar are handled by two different rules, and see which question you have to ask first to get both right.

explanationHtml:
What is going on

Maltese has one word for "the", but it is spelled several different ways: il, li, l, and forms like is, iċ, ir, iż, id. Nothing about the meaning of the noun matters here - only the sounds the noun begins with. This is a phonological rule: the shape of one word changes because of the sounds next to it. (English does something similar in a small way: a before a consonant, an before a vowel.)

Step 1: group the data by article

Looking at the 22 examples:

  • The article's l turns into a copy of the noun's first consonant in is sħana, iċ ċpar, id dar, iż żir, ir raġel, is silġ. The consonants that trigger this are s, ċ, d, ż, r - and if you look them up in the chart, every single one sits in the Alveolar column (made with the tip of the tongue). This copying is called assimilation.
  • The bare form l appears in l art, l uffiċċju (nouns starting with a vowel), l għonq (għ is silent, so what you actually hear first is a vowel), and l jum (j counts as a vowel-like sound here).
  • li appears in li mħadda, li ksieħ, li ħmar, li bdiewa - each of these begins with two consonants in a row (a consonant cluster). The extra vowel makes the mouthful easier to say.
  • il appears everywhere else: il lanġas, il mara, il bar, il lvant, il vjola, il qassis - single non-alveolar consonants.

Step 2: put the rules in order

The rules overlap, so they have to be tried one after another, top first:

  1. Before an alveolar consonant, the article's consonant becomes a copy of it (assimilation).
  2. Otherwise, before a vowel or a silent letter, use the bare form with no vowel.
  3. Otherwise, before a consonant cluster, use the form with a vowel after the l.
  4. Otherwise, use the default form.

Order matters. ir raġel starts with a single alveolar r, so rule 1 fires. li ħmar starts with ħ, which is pharyngeal and not alveolar, so rule 1 fails, ħ is a real (pronounced) consonant so rule 2 fails, and ħm is a cluster, so rule 3 gives li. Note also il lvant: l and r are alveolar, so rule 1 should apply - and it does, in a hidden way, since a copy of l is just l again, which is why it looks like the default form.

Step 3: the two exceptions (A1)

il ktieb begins with the cluster kt, so the rules predict the li form, but the data shows the default form instead. il ġobon begins with ġ, which the chart lists as an alveolar affricate (it is simply the voiced partner of ċ), so assimilation should have applied - and indeed the answer sheet for ġebla shows that it normally does. So the two rule-breakers are ktieb and ġobon.

Step 4: applying the rules to the new nouns

Work through the first letter of each:

  • xkora, xemx: x is an alveolar fricative, so rule 1 - even though xkora also starts a cluster, rule 1 comes first.
  • ġebla, tama, nar, nifs, dlam: ġ, t, n, d are all alveolar, so rule 1 again (and dlam and nifs being clusters does not matter).
  • hena, għajn: h and għ are silent, so rule 2. ors, ilma: begin with vowels, rule 2 as well.
  • mniħer: m is labial, pronounced, and mn is a cluster - rule 3.
  • kafè, missier, beraq: single non-alveolar consonants, rule 4. lura: l is alveolar, so rule 1 technically applies, but copying l gives l, so the result looks like the default form.

Why linguists care

The same split exists in Arabic, Maltese's ancestor: the consonants that trigger assimilation of the article are traditionally called sun letters (from xemx, "sun") and the rest moon letters (from qamar, "moon"). The class is not an arbitrary list - it is exactly the set of sounds made with the tip of the tongue, the same place the article's own l is made, which is what makes the copying easy for the mouth to do.

A1: the booklet asks for two words on the answer sheet; transcribed here as ONE question whose key is the solution's wording 'ktieb and ġobon' - if the official answer sheet prints two separate lines, this may need splitting into A1.1/A1.2. Points split is an assumption (A1 = 2, A2 = 16 x 0.5); the solution shows no per-part breakdown. Please verify the diacritics in the data (ġ, ħ, ż, ċ, għ, è) against the PDF.
